subject: physics
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: What are the voltage and frequency of the UK mains electricity supply?
questions.explain: UK mains is supplied at approximately 230 V with an alternating frequency of 50 Hz.

questions.q: In a UK three-pin plug, what colour is the insulation on the live wire?
questions.explain: The live wire is brown, the neutral is blue and the earth is green and yellow.

questions.q: What colour is the insulation on the earth wire in a UK mains plug?
questions.explain: The earth wire uses green-and-yellow striped insulation as a safety connection to the ground.

questions.q: Why is a metal-cased appliance connected to the earth wire and fitted with a fuse?
options: If the live wire touches the case, a large current flows to earth and blows the fuse, disconnecting the supply
The earth wire increases the appliance's power output
The fuse stores charge to keep the appliance running during a power cut
The earth wire makes the current alternate more smoothly
questions.explain: Earthing plus a fuse ensures a fault causes a surge that melts the fuse, cutting off the supply before the case becomes dangerous.

questions.q: An appliance operates from the 230 V mains and draws a current of 2 A. What is its power?
questions.explain: Power P = I x V = 2 x 230 = 460 W.

questions.q: The UK mains supply is best described as which type of current?
questions.explain: Mains electricity is alternating current, repeatedly reversing direction 50 times per second.

questions.q: Some appliances with plastic cases are described as double insulated. Why do they not need an earth wire?
options: The plastic case cannot become live, so there is no need for an earth connection
Plastic conducts electricity safely to the ground
They use direct current instead of alternating current
The fuse is built into the plastic case instead
questions.explain: Double-insulated appliances have non-conducting cases, so the case can never become live and earthing is unnecessary.

questions.q: What is the SI unit of electrical resistance?
questions.explain: Resistance is measured in ohms, symbol capital omega.

questions.q: Which equation correctly relates resistance R, voltage V and current I?
questions.explain: Resistance equals the voltage across a component divided by the current through it.

questions.q: Two lamps are connected in series in a circuit. How does the current compare at different points?
options: The current is the same at every point in the series circuit
The current is largest just after the battery and decreases around the loop
The current splits equally between the two lamps
The current is zero between the two lamps
questions.explain: In a series circuit there is only one path, so the current has the same value everywhere.

questions.q: Two identical resistors are connected in parallel across a battery. What is true of the voltage across each resistor?
options: Each resistor has the same voltage, equal to the battery voltage
The battery voltage is shared equally between them
The voltage across each is half the battery voltage
The voltage is zero across one and full across the other
questions.explain: Components in parallel are connected across the same two points, so they share the same potential difference.

questions.q: A resistor has a voltage of 12 V across it and a current of 3 A flowing through it. What is its resistance?
questions.explain: R = V / I = 12 / 3 = 4 ohms.

questions.q: How does the resistance of a filament lamp change as the current through it increases?
options: The resistance increases because the filament gets hotter
The resistance stays constant because it obeys Ohm's law
The resistance decreases because the filament gets hotter
The resistance falls to zero once it lights up
questions.explain: A larger current heats the filament, and the higher temperature raises its resistance, giving a curved I-V graph.

questions.q: What is the key electrical behaviour of a diode?
options: It only allows current to flow in one direction
It allows current to flow equally in both directions
Its resistance decreases as light falls on it
It stores charge like a battery
questions.explain: A diode has very high resistance in the reverse direction, so current flows through it in one direction only.

questions.q: The equation V = W / Q describes voltage (potential difference). What does it tell us that voltage represents?
options: The energy transferred per unit of charge passing through
The charge stored per unit of energy
The resistance per unit of charge
questions.explain: Potential difference is the energy transferred per coulomb of charge, so V = W / Q.

questions.q: What is the SI unit of electric charge?
questions.explain: Electric charge is measured in coulombs, symbol C.

questions.q: Two objects carry the same type of electric charge. What force do they exert on each other?
options: They exert no force at all
questions.explain: Like charges repel and unlike charges attract.

questions.q: A current of 0.5 A flows for 20 seconds. How much charge passes a point in the circuit?
questions.explain: Charge Q = I x t = 0.5 x 20 = 10 C.

questions.q: When a polythene rod is rubbed with a cloth it becomes negatively charged. What has happened?
options: Electrons have been transferred from the cloth onto the rod
Protons have moved from the cloth onto the rod
Electrons have moved from the rod onto the cloth
The rod has gained extra neutrons
questions.explain: Friction transfers electrons; gaining electrons gives the rod an overall negative charge.

questions.q: A 100 W lamp is switched on for 60 seconds. How much electrical energy does it transfer?
questions.explain: Energy transferred E = P x t = 100 x 60 = 6000 J.
